title: File Processing and Exception Handling
overview: Write code to open, read, write and close files in READ, WRITE, APPEND and RANDOM modes, and process serial, sequential and random files of records. Know what an exception is, why handling it stops a program crashing, when handling is appropriate, and write TRY/EXCEPT code. Sections follow coursebook chapter 26.
syllabusPoints: Write code to perform file-processing operations: open a file in read, write or append mode and close it.
Read a record from a file and write a record to a file.
Perform file-processing operations on serial, sequential and random files.
Show understanding of an exception and the importance of exception handling.
Know when it is appropriate to use exception handling.
Write program code to use exception handling.

definitions.definition: An unexpected event that occurs while a program is running and causes it to halt (a run-time error), e.g. division by zero, end of file, hardware failure.
A routine that responds to unexpected events while the program runs, trapping run-time errors so the program does not halt and giving a meaningful error message.
A user-defined data type made of fields, which may have different data types, one of which is normally the key.
A file whose records are stored in the order they were added, with no key order.
A file whose records are stored in order of a key field and read from the start.
A file that stores records at specific addresses so they can be accessed directly.
How a file is opened: READ (read only), WRITE (new file, existing data lost), APPEND (add to the end) or RANDOM (direct access).
The condition when no more data can be read; EOF(file) returns TRUE then.
The position in the file where the next read or write happens; SEEK moves it to a given address.
A file storing data in its internal binary form (e.g. whole records) rather than as lines of text.

sections.title: Records (coursebook 26.01)
content: Files of records store one record per entity, so first define the record. A record is a user-defined type grouping fields of different types; an array of records holds many.
bullets: Record: a user-defined composite data type with fields that may have different data types.
One field is the key (e.g. VehicleID): it uniquely identifies the record and decides its position in a sequential or random file.
Declare the type first (TYPE ... ENDTYPE), then variables of that type, then arrays of that type.
Fields are reached with dot notation: ThisCar.EngineSize.
Python has no record type: a class holding only attributes set in the constructor is used (Java also uses a class with no methods).
Records stored in a file must have the same fields in the same order, so each can be read back reliably.

examples.label: Declaring a record and an array of records
examples.content:
TYPE CarRecord
    DECLARE VehicleID : STRING      // key field
    DECLARE Registration : STRING
    DECLARE EngineSize : INTEGER
    DECLARE PurchasePrice : REAL
ENDTYPE

DECLARE ThisCar : CarRecord
DECLARE Car : ARRAY[1:100] OF CarRecord
ThisCar.EngineSize ← 2500
Car[2].EngineSize ← 1600

examples.label: A class used as a record
examples.content:
class CarRecord:
    def __init__(self):
        self.vehicle_id = ""
        self.registration = ""
        self.engine_size = 0
        self.price = 0.0

cars = [CarRecord() for _ in range(3)]
cars[0].vehicle_id = "V01"
cars[0].engine_size = 1600
print(cars[0].vehicle_id, cars[0].engine_size, cars[1].engine_size)

sections.title: File operations and modes (26.02)
content: A file must be opened in one mode, used, then closed. The mode says what the program intends to do, and the wrong one can destroy data.
bullets: OPENFILE <file> FOR READ: data is read from an existing file; the file is not changed.
OPENFILE <file> FOR WRITE: creates a new file; any existing data in the file is lost (overwritten).
OPENFILE <file> FOR APPEND: new data is added after the existing data at the end of the file.
OPENFILE <file> FOR RANDOM: records are read and written directly at a chosen address.
A file is opened in only one mode at a time. Close it with CLOSEFILE when finished so data is saved and the file is released.
READFILE <file>, <variable>: reads the next line into a STRING variable. WRITEFILE <file>, <data>: writes a line.
EOF(<file>) returns TRUE when there are no more lines to read (or the file is empty) and FALSE otherwise; loop WHILE NOT EOF(<file>).
Text file: lines of text read or written serially as strings. Binary file: stores data in its internal form, used for records.
Operations on records in a binary file: PUTRECORD <file>, <record> writes a record; GETRECORD <file>, <record> reads one; SEEK <file>, <address> moves to a record.
Python: open(name, mode) with r, w, a for text; add b for binary (rb, wb); r+ or w+ for read and write. Reading a missing file in r mode raises FileNotFoundError.
Use a with block so the file is closed even when an exception occurs.

examples.label: Text file: copy lines, then append a footer
examples.content:
DECLARE Line : STRING
OPENFILE "Names.txt" FOR READ
OPENFILE "Upper.txt" FOR WRITE
WHILE NOT EOF("Names.txt")
    READFILE "Names.txt", Line
    WRITEFILE "Upper.txt", UCASE(Line)
ENDWHILE
CLOSEFILE "Names.txt"
CLOSEFILE "Upper.txt"

OPENFILE "Upper.txt" FOR APPEND
WRITEFILE "Upper.txt", "END OF LIST"
CLOSEFILE "Upper.txt"

examples.label: Write, append and read text records
examples.content:
with open("students.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    file.write("A104,Ari,72\n")
    file.write("A219,Bao,81\n")

with open("students.txt", "a", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    file.write("A315,Chau,68\n")

with open("students.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    for line in file:
        print(line.rstrip("\n"))

sections.title: Serial and sequential files
content: Both kinds are read from the start, one record after another. They differ only in how the records are ordered.
bullets: Serial file: records are stored in the order they were added (chronological), not sorted by any key.
Sequential file: records are stored in order of a key field (e.g. ascending VehicleID).
Adding to a serial file: APPEND the new record at the end. Adding to a sequential file: the record must go in its correct place, so a new version of the file is written.
To update, insert or delete in a sequential file: read the old file, copy records to a new file with the change made, then replace the old file with the new one.
Searching either file means reading records from the first until the key is found or the file ends (EOF). A sequential file can stop early once a key greater than the target is read.
Saving an array of records: OPENFILE FOR WRITE, loop PUTRECORD for each element, CLOSEFILE. Restoring: OPENFILE FOR READ, loop GETRECORD, CLOSEFILE.
Reading binary records back needs an end-of-file check, or an EOF exception, otherwise the program crashes at the end.
Suitable for: backups, logs, batch processing of every record (e.g. a payroll run). Unsuitable when a single record must be found quickly.

examples.label: Saving and restoring an array of records
examples.content:
OPENFILE "CarFile.dat" FOR WRITE
FOR i ← 1 TO 100
    PUTRECORD "CarFile.dat", Car[i]
NEXT i
CLOSEFILE "CarFile.dat"

OPENFILE "CarFile.dat" FOR READ
FOR i ← 1 TO 100
    GETRECORD "CarFile.dat", Car[i]
NEXT i
CLOSEFILE "CarFile.dat"

examples.label: Serial binary file of records using pickle
Search an ascending sequential file
Insert and delete in a sequential file by writing a new version
examples.content:
import os

def insert_sorted(filename, new_line):
    inserted = False
    with open(filename, "r", encoding="utf-8") as old, \
         open(filename + ".new", "w", encoding="utf-8") as new:
        for line in old:
            if not inserted and line > new_line:
                new.write(new_line)
                inserted = True
            new.write(line)
        if not inserted:
            new.write(new_line)
    os.replace(filename + ".new", filename)

def delete_student(filename, target_id):
    with open(filename, "r", encoding="utf-8") as old, \
         open(filename + ".new", "w", encoding="utf-8") as new:
        for line in old:
            if not line.startswith(target_id + ","):
                new.write(line)
    os.replace(filename + ".new", filename)

insert_sorted("students.txt", "A250,Dev,90\n")
print(open("students.txt").read().splitlines())
delete_student("students.txt", "A104")
print(open("students.txt").read().splitlines())

sections.title: Random-access files
content: A random (direct-access) file stores records at specific addresses, so one record can be read or written without reading the ones before it. The address is usually worked out from the key.
bullets: Random file: stores records at specific addresses that can be accessed directly.
Records are fixed length, so a record's position can be calculated: address = record number x record size (numbering from 0).
SEEK <file>, <address> moves the file pointer to the record's address.
GETRECORD reads the record at the pointer into a variable of the record type. PUTRECORD writes the variable into the record at the pointer, replacing what was there.
After GETRECORD or PUTRECORD the pointer moves to the next record, so SEEK again before each access.
Update in situ: SEEK to the record, GETRECORD, change the field, SEEK again, PUTRECORD it back in the same place.
Address from the key: a hashing algorithm gives the record's address (e.g. key MOD number of slots). Two keys can give the same address (a collision), so store in the next free slot.
To find a record: calculate the address, SEEK, GETRECORD, compare the key; if it differs, check the next slots until the key or an empty slot is found.
Fast for finding or updating one record; but space is wasted if slots are empty, and the file is not in key order for processing every record.
A random file must be opened in a mode that allows reading and writing (RANDOM; in Python r+b or w+b), and an answer should explain how addresses are calculated.

examples.label: Store and retrieve with an address calculated from the key
examples.content:
CONSTANT Slots = 1000
FUNCTION Slot(CustomerID : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER
    RETURN CustomerID MOD Slots
ENDFUNCTION

DECLARE Cust : CustomerRecord
DECLARE Temp : CustomerRecord
OPENFILE "Customers.dat" FOR RANDOM

// store: next free slot if the first one is taken (0 = empty)
Address ← Slot(Cust.CustomerID)
SEEK "Customers.dat", Address
GETRECORD "Customers.dat", Temp
WHILE Temp.CustomerID <> 0
    Address ← (Address + 1) MOD Slots
    SEEK "Customers.dat", Address
    GETRECORD "Customers.dat", Temp
ENDWHILE
SEEK "Customers.dat", Address
PUTRECORD "Customers.dat", Cust

// retrieve one record by its slot
SEEK "Customers.dat", Slot(KeyWanted)
GETRECORD "Customers.dat", Cust
CLOSEFILE "Customers.dat"

examples.label: Trace: 10 slots, address = key MOD 10
examples.content:
Keys stored in this order: 100234, 100244, 100305, 100314, 100899
100234  MOD 10 = 4  slot 4 empty            -> stored in slot 4
100244  MOD 10 = 4  slot 4 full, 5 empty    -> stored in slot 5
100305  MOD 10 = 5  slot 5 full, 6 empty    -> stored in slot 6
100314  MOD 10 = 4  slots 4, 5, 6 full      -> stored in slot 7
100899  MOD 10 = 9  slot 9 empty            -> stored in slot 9
Finding 100314: start at slot 4 (100234), 5 (100244), 6 (100305), 7 found: 4 reads.

examples.label: Fixed-length records: write, read and update in place
examples.content:
import struct

RECORD = struct.Struct("<6s20sf")  # id, name, balance = 30 bytes

def put_record(file, number, rec_id, name, balance):
    file.seek(number * RECORD.size)
    file.write(RECORD.pack(rec_id.encode(), name.encode(), balance))

def get_record(file, number):
    file.seek(number * RECORD.size)
    raw = file.read(RECORD.size)
    if len(raw) < RECORD.size:
        return None
    rec_id, name, balance = RECORD.unpack(raw)
    return rec_id.rstrip(b"\0").decode(), name.rstrip(b"\0").decode(), balance

with open("accounts.dat", "w+b") as file:
    for i in range(10):
        put_record(file, i, "", "", 0.0)
    put_record(file, 234 % 10, "100234", "Ari", 50.0)
    rec = get_record(file, 4)
    put_record(file, 4, rec[0], rec[1], rec[2] + 25.5)
    print(get_record(file, 4), get_record(file, 3), get_record(file, 10))

sections.title: Exceptions and exception handling (26.03)
content: Programs meet situations they cannot control. Without a response the program stops; exception handling lets it respond sensibly.
bullets: Exception: an unexpected event that occurs during the execution of a program and causes it to halt (run-time error).

Examples: end of file reached unexpectedly, a programming or user error (e.g. text typed where a number is needed, array index out of range), hardware failure (e.g. disk or network fails), division by zero, file not found.
Exception handling: code (an exception handling routine) that responds to an unexpected event while the program is running.
It traps the run-time error so the program does not halt unexpectedly.
It produces a meaningful error message for the user instead of the system crash message.
It lets the program recover (ask again, use a default, skip the record) or close down safely, saving data and closing files.
Pseudocode structure: TRY <statements> EXCEPT <handler statements> ENDTRY. Any run-time error in the TRY block is caught and the EXCEPT block runs.
More than one EXCEPT block can be used, each for a different type of exception. An optional FINALLY block runs whether or not an exception occurred.
TRY, EXCEPT and FINALLY come from the coursebook; the 2026 pseudocode guide does not list them, so state the structure clearly or answer in the programming language.
Python types: FileNotFoundError / IOError (file cannot be opened), ValueError (inappropriate value), ZeroDivisionError, EOFError (end of file met while reading), ImportError, KeyboardInterrupt.

examples.label: Handling a filename that does not exist
examples.content:
OUTPUT "Which file do you want to use? "
INPUT FileName
TRY
    OPENFILE FileName FOR RANDOM
EXCEPT
    OUTPUT "File " & FileName & " could not be opened"
ENDTRY

sections.title: When to use exception handling
content: Use it for events that can happen even when the code is correct, outside the program's control. Do not use it to hide bugs.
bullets: Appropriate: opening a file that may not exist or be locked, reading to the end of a file, unpredictable user input, a network or device failure.
Appropriate when the error cannot be fully prevented by a check beforehand, or a check would be longer than a handler.
Not a substitute for testing, for easy validation (e.g. a range check) or for fixing logic errors.
Catch the specific exception you can deal with; a bare catch-all hides faults and makes bugs hard to find.
In a handler, either recover (ask again, default value) or report clearly and stop safely.
Always release resources: close files in FINALLY or use a with block.

analysisChains.title: Why a missing file should be handled by an exception handler
steps: The user types a filename that does not exist
Opening it raises an exception (run-time error)
Unhandled, the program halts with a system message and unsaved work is lost
A handler traps the error, shows a meaningful message and lets the program ask again or end safely
analysisChains.evaluation: Handling is right here as the file's existence is outside the program's control; checking first can still fail if the file is removed in between.

analysisChains.title: Why a random file needs fixed-length records
steps: A record's address is calculated as number x record size
That only works if every record is the same size
SEEK can then jump straight to the record without reading earlier ones
GETRECORD and PUTRECORD read or replace exactly one record in place
analysisChains.evaluation: Quick access to one record, at the cost of wasted space in empty or short records.

analysisChains.title: Why updating a sequential file means writing a new file
steps: Records are kept in key order
A new record must go between two existing records
There is no space to insert, so records after it would have to move
The old file is copied to a new file with the record added, then replaced
analysisChains.evaluation: Simple and keeps the order but slow for large files; a random file avoids rewriting.

examTips: WRITE mode destroys existing data; to add records say APPEND. A common 1-mark answer is that WRITE overwrites.
Give the mode, the operation and CLOSEFILE: OPENFILE name FOR READ ... CLOSEFILE name. Missing CLOSEFILE loses a mark.
Reading loops: WHILE NOT EOF(file) with READFILE inside; do not test EOF after the read.
Random files: always SEEK before GETRECORD or PUTRECORD and say how the address is calculated.

Define an exception as 'an unexpected event during execution that causes the program to halt'. For 2 examples give any two of end of file, user or programming error, hardware failure, division by zero.
Exception handling: say it traps run-time errors, stops the program halting, and gives a meaningful error message (3 marks).
In code, name the exception type you catch (FileNotFoundError, ValueError), not an empty except.
commonMistakes: Opening an existing file in WRITE mode and wiping its data when APPEND was needed.
Forgetting to close the file, or closing it only on the path with no error.
Reading past the end of the file because EOF was not tested (or EOFError not caught).
Using SEEK with a random file of variable-length records, so addresses are wrong.
Saying exception handling 'fixes' the error; it traps and responds to it.
Catching every exception with one bare except and hiding programming errors.
Using exception handling in place of a simple check such as a range check.

quickRecall.question: What is an exception?
quickRecall.answer: An unexpected event during the execution of a program that causes it to halt (a run-time error).

quickRecall.question: Give two examples of exceptions.
quickRecall.answer: Any two of: end of file, user/programming error, hardware failure, division by zero.

quickRecall.question: What does an exception handling routine do?
quickRecall.answer: Responds to unexpected events while the program runs: it traps run-time errors, stops the program halting unexpectedly and gives a meaningful error message.

quickRecall.question: What is the difference between WRITE and APPEND mode?
quickRecall.answer: WRITE creates a new file and loses existing data; APPEND adds new data after the existing data.

quickRecall.question: Which pseudocode statement tests for the end of a file?
quickRecall.answer: EOF(<file>): TRUE when there are no more lines to read.

quickRecall.question: How do serial and sequential files differ?
quickRecall.answer: Serial records are in the order added; sequential records are in key order.

quickRecall.question: What do SEEK, GETRECORD and PUTRECORD do?
quickRecall.answer: SEEK moves to a record's address; GETRECORD reads the record there; PUTRECORD writes a record there.

quickRecall.question: Why must random file records be fixed length?
quickRecall.answer: So a record's address can be calculated (number x size) and SEEK can jump straight to it.

quickRecall.question: What does a FINALLY block do?
quickRecall.answer: Its statements run whether or not an exception occurred, e.g. to close a file.
